subject: sacks

brief.inclusion: Technology investor, political fundraiser and former White House AI and cryptocurrency adviser who translated a Silicon Valley political network into federal technology policy.
brief.namesakes: Do not confuse David Oliver Sacks, the Craft Ventures partner born in Cape Town in 1972, with television writer David Sacks or psychologist David Neil Sacks.

summary: David Sacks built his wealth as PayPal's operating chief, founder of Yammer and co-founder of Craft Ventures, then became a political fundraiser and media voice through the All-In podcast. After helping move a group of technology investors toward Donald Trump in 2024, he served as the White House AI and cryptocurrency adviser in 2025–2026, co-authored the administration's AI Action Plan and moved to an outside advisory role as co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.

chapters.title: From Cape Town to Stanford
chapters.dek: Migration, elite education and a campus conservative network supplied the first institutions of Sacks's career.
chapters.body:
David Oliver Sacks was born in Cape Town on May 25, 1972, into a Jewish family and moved to Tennessee when he was five. He attended Memphis University School, then studied economics at Stanford, graduating in 1994. At Stanford he joined the conservative Stanford Review and formed a working relationship with Peter Thiel, who had founded the paper. [[forward-sacks-2023, atlantic-sacks-2026]]

Sacks and Thiel published The Diversity Myth in 1995, arguing that multicultural policy and political correctness had narrowed debate on campus. Some of Sacks's student writing has drawn later criticism, and he has expressed regret for parts of it. The episode matters because it established a recurring method: treating cultural conflict as a struggle over institutional power and speech rather than only personal opinion. [[independent-diversity-myth, atlantic-sacks-2026]]

After earning a law degree at the University of Chicago in 1998, Sacks briefly worked in consulting. He did not build a legal career. Instead, he returned to the Stanford network just as its members were moving from campus argument into internet companies. [[craft-bio, atlantic-sacks-2026]]

chapters.title: The PayPal operating network
chapters.dek: At PayPal, Sacks acquired both operating credibility and a network that later crossed business, media and politics.
chapters.body:
In 1999 Sacks joined Confinity, the payments company led by Thiel and Max Levchin that became PayPal. He led product work and later served as chief operating officer, overseeing functions that included product, sales, marketing and operations. The job made him an operator inside one of the defining firms of the dot-com period rather than simply an early investor. [[craft-bio, atlantic-sacks-2026]]

EBay announced its agreement to buy PayPal for about $1.5 billion in July 2002. The transaction dispersed a group of employees and founders into new companies and funds, while preserving relationships among Thiel, Sacks, Elon Musk and other alumni. That network supplied Sacks with capital, reputation and access for the companies and investments that followed. [[ebay-paypal-2002, craft-bio, time-sacks-2024]]

chapters.title: Yammer created independent wealth
chapters.dek: A successful enterprise-software company gave Sacks an exit separate from the collective PayPal story.
chapters.body:
Sacks founded Yammer in 2008 as an internal communications service for businesses. The product applied social-network mechanics to workplace collaboration, and Sacks served as chief executive as it expanded across corporate customers. [[craft-bio, microsoft-yammer-2012]]

Microsoft agreed in June 2012 to acquire Yammer for $1.2 billion in cash. The sale was Sacks's defining independent business outcome: it supplied wealth and a founder's record that later supported his authority as an investor and commentator on how technology firms should be built. [[microsoft-yammer-2012]]

After Yammer, Sacks invested in startups and briefly ran Zenefits during a regulatory crisis. In 2017 he co-founded Craft Ventures, converting his personal investing into a firm. Craft's portfolio and Sacks's continued management role later became central to conflict-of-interest questions when he entered government. [[craft-bio, atlantic-sacks-2026]]

chapters.title: A microphone became a political institution
chapters.dek: All-In turned investor conversations into a durable platform for campaigns and policy arguments.
chapters.body:
Sacks began co-hosting All-In in 2020 with Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis and David Friedberg. What began as a technology and markets discussion became a high-reach forum for elections, war, censorship, cryptocurrency and artificial intelligence. The show joined Sacks's capital network to a media audience without the institutional filters of a newspaper or television network. [[all-in-about, washpost-sacks-2025]]

His politics did not move in a straight line toward Trump. After January 6, 2021, Sacks said Trump had disqualified himself from another national candidacy. In the 2024 Republican primary he initially backed Ron DeSantis and joined Elon Musk to host DeSantis's troubled Twitter Spaces launch in May 2023. [[time-sacks-2024, forward-desantis-launch-2023]]

Across the same period, Sacks argued that technology platforms and government pressure were restricting speech, criticized the Biden administration's approach to cryptocurrency and questioned U.S. strategy in Ukraine. Those positions brought his podcast audience, investment relationships and political activity into the same public identity. [[washpost-sacks-2025, atlantic-sacks-2026]]

chapters.title: The turn to Trump
chapters.dek: Fundraising converted a media and investor network into campaign infrastructure.
chapters.body:
By June 2024 Sacks had moved from his post-January 6 rejection of Trump to active support. He and Palihapitiya hosted Trump at Sacks's San Francisco home for a fundraiser reported to have raised roughly $12 million. The event did not represent all of Silicon Valley, but it provided visible evidence that a group of major technology investors was willing to organize money and elite validation for the Republican nominee. [[fox-sacks-fundraiser-2024, washpost-sacks-2025]]

Sacks spoke at the Republican National Convention and helped connect JD Vance with technology donors. Trump also appeared on All-In, bringing the candidate into the program's business-and-technology frame. Sacks argued that a Trump administration would be more favorable to innovation, crypto and political speech. [[time-sacks-2024, washpost-sacks-2025]]

Federal contributions capture only part of this political role. Hosting, introductions, media advocacy and the ability to assemble other donors are not equivalent to personal checks and do not appear as a single FEC total, so the dossier keeps those forms of influence separate. [[fec-sacks, washpost-sacks-2025]]

chapters.title: A new kind of White House appointment
chapters.dek: The special-government-employee structure put an active venture capitalist inside technology policy without Senate confirmation.
chapters.body:
On December 5, 2024, Trump announced Sacks as White House AI and crypto adviser. The role did not require Senate confirmation. Sacks entered as a special government employee, a status generally limited to 130 service days in a year, and the July 2025 staff report listed him at no salary. [[trump-sacks-appointment-2024, white-house-staff-2025]]

The appointment joined two policy fields in which private investment and public rules can rapidly change company values. Sacks retained his role at Craft while working on broad federal policy. Supporters argued that government needed an experienced technology operator; critics argued that the arrangement gave an investor unusual access to decisions affecting his industry. [[time-sacks-2024, washpost-sacks-2025, warren-sacks-letter-2025]]

chapters.title: Divestments did not end the ethics debate
chapters.dek: White House waivers documented large sales while permitting work on policies affecting broad sectors.
chapters.body:
A March 2025 White House memorandum said Sacks and Craft had sold liquid cryptocurrency and numerous direct and fund interests connected to digital assets. A later memorandum addressed artificial-intelligence holdings. The documents described extensive divestments and allowed Sacks to participate in matters of general applicability even when broad policy could affect firms in which he or Craft retained interests. [[white-house-crypto-waiver-2025, white-house-ai-waiver-2025]]

The waivers narrowed direct conflicts but did not settle the larger question of an investor shaping rules for industries in which his professional network remained active. Senator Elizabeth Warren sought records about his holdings, waivers and number of government-service days. Her letter raised allegations and questions; it was not a legal finding that Sacks had violated ethics law. [[warren-sacks-letter-2025]]

Sacks and his defenders said the service imposed substantial personal costs and that divestments insulated his work. Critical reporting argued that sector-wide policy could still benefit Craft's ecosystem and allied investors. The public record therefore supports two distinct facts: significant divestment occurred, and disagreement about the adequacy of the remaining safeguards continued. [[white-house-crypto-waiver-2025, white-house-ai-waiver-2025, atlantic-sacks-2026]]

chapters.title: AI acceleration and crypto normalization
chapters.dek: Sacks's policy record centered on reducing barriers, building infrastructure and treating technology competition as national strategy.
chapters.body:
The July 2025 AI Action Plan, signed by Sacks, Michael Kratsios and Marco Rubio, organized more than ninety proposed federal actions under innovation, infrastructure and international leadership. It called for faster data-center and energy development, wider export of American AI systems and removal of federal rules the administration considered ideological or unnecessarily restrictive. [[white-house-ai-plan-2025, white-house-ai-plan-release-2025]]

The plan framed competition with China as an economic and military race while rejecting both unrestricted use and the strongest catastrophe-focused regulatory proposals. It said AI should complement workers, avoid ideological bias and be protected from theft and misuse. Critics argued that the acceleration agenda discounted safety, labor and concentration risks; those criticisms were part of the policy dispute, not proof that a specific harm had occurred. [[white-house-ai-plan-2025, atlantic-sacks-2026]]

On cryptocurrency, Sacks coordinated with a presidential working group that proposed market-structure, banking and regulatory changes. Industry participants welcomed the reversal from enforcement-led policy, while ethics critics pointed to the administration's and advisers' private financial ties. [[white-house-digital-assets-2025, ap-crypto-policy-2025, warren-sacks-letter-2025]]

chapters.title: Outside the payroll, still inside the policy network
chapters.dek: The end of Sacks's temporary appointment changed his legal status more than his access.
chapters.body:
Trump appointed Sacks and Kratsios to co-chair the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology on March 25, 2026. The next day Sacks said he had used the permitted days of his special-government-employee role and was leaving the formal AI-and-crypto post. Reuters reported that he would continue helping advance the administration's AI framework. [[white-house-pcast-2026, reuters-sacks-stepdown-2026]]

The transition captured the structure of Sacks's political power. He did not need a permanent agency or Senate-confirmed office to remain useful to the president. His leverage came from combining access to investors and founders, a media platform, fundraising credibility and a policy program that the administration had already adopted. [[reuters-sacks-stepdown-2026, atlantic-sacks-2026]]

As of October 2026, Sacks remained a Craft partner, All-In co-host and PCAST co-chair rather than the salaried head of a regulatory agency. That distinction matters: he advises and organizes, while cabinet departments and independent agencies retain legal authority to implement or contest the policies associated with him. [[craft-bio, all-in-about, white-house-pcast-2026]]
